title: Irishman charged with destroying US military aircraft with axe
description: US officials have charged an Irishman with destroying a $60m (£45m) American military aircraft after he allegedly snuck onto the tarmac of an airport
body: US officials have charged an Irishman with destroying a $60m (£45m) American military aircraft after he allegedly snuck onto the tarmac of an airport in Ireland. Daithi O'Corrain, 48, is accused of doing extensive research before he allegedly used chemicals and various tools - including an axe - to damage a US Air National Guard C-130 Hercules parked at Shannon Airport near Limerick. American prosecutors have charged him with destruction of government property, which carries a maximum sentence of 10 years in prison.O'Corrain is not currently in US custody, according to the Associated Press news agency, and it is unclear whether he has a lawyer who could speak on his behalf.In filings unsealed by prosecutors in New York on Tuesday, agents from the FBI argued that the act jeopardised US national security. They say the plane was parked at the airport while en route to another country on a US military assignment."As alleged, Daithi O'Corrain carried out a deliberate, planned attack against a US military aircraft, causing tens of millions of dollars in damage and jeopardizing critical military operations," prosecutors said in a court filing. "This was not an act of spontaneous vandalism," said FBI Assistant Director in Charge James Barnacle Jr, explaining O'Corrain "spent months researching the aircraft, acquiring tools and materials, and preparing to maximize the destruction he could inflict."Officials say that the suspect planned extensively for the 11 April 2026 raid, and brought tools with him for the demolition, which took place over several hours.He entered the plane by breaking a locking mechanism, officials say, then used straps to close the doors before covering the windows. "O'Corrain then proceeded to inflict severe damage to the interior of the Aircraft by, among other things, cutting wire bundles and hydraulic lines within the Aircraft, crimping a liquid oxygen line within the Aircraft, destroying every gauge in the Aircraft's cockpit, and puncturing the Aircraft's air ducts," the US indictment says.He also used gallium, a substance that can erode aluminum and steel, ball bearings which he poured in the fuel tank, and an axe which he used to puncture the exterior of the plane.He was caught by airport crew, and filmed standing on top of the plane. He was arrested at the scene, and charged by Ireland's national police with causing criminal damages.

schema.headline: Irishman charged with destroying US military aircraft with axe

title: Largest British study to check social media ban's effect on youth mental health
description: The work, funded by health charity The Wellcome Trust, will help inform future online safety policies in the UK and internationally, with some early r
body: The work, funded by health charity The Wellcome Trust, will help inform future online safety policies in the UK and internationally, with some early results available before the ban happens. Researchers will use wearable technology, smartphones, digital diaries and surveys to collect data to see how young people respond to the ban, both physically and mentally.And they will check whether young people find ways to circumvent restrictions.Dr Camilla Iannone, research lead at Wellcome, said it was a once-in-a-generation opportunity to study at scale how social media and its restrictions affected youth mental health."We really don't think that this is a simple binary question of whether social media is good or bad, or whether restrictions work or don't work."Instead, the teams will study whether changing young people's digital environment leads to meaningful changes in their mental health and wellbeing."Participants are being recruited to reflect a diverse range of young people, including different genders and sexual orientations. People with existing mental health conditions, such as anxiety and depression, will also be included, as well as young people who are neurodivergent. Groups have been set up at Cardiff University, the University of Oxford, the University of Birmingham, King's College London, the University of Edinburgh, the University of Manchester, the London School of Hygiene and Tropical Medicine, and University College London.

schema.headline: Largest British study to check social media ban's effect on youth mental health

title: American soldier arrested in UK taken into US military custody
description: American soldier arrested by UK police on suspicion of spying taken into US military custodyImage source, FacebookImage caption, Lt Col Brandon Carrol
body: American soldier arrested by UK police on suspicion of spying taken into US military custodyImage source, FacebookImage caption, Lt Col Brandon Carroll Tyner was arrested on 10 November ByHafsa Khalil and Daniel SandfordUK correspondentA US Army officer arrested in the UK on suspicion of spying for Russia earlier this month has been taken into US military custody, British counter-terror police have said.The serviceman has been identified as Lt Col Brandon Carroll Tyner, BBC News understands. The 41-year-old - who served in the US Army since 2008 - was arrested near Gloucester last week by British counter-terror police. Tyner was based at Imjin Barracks in Innsworth, Gloucestershire, the headquarters of Nato's Allied Rapid Reaction Corps.Counter Terrorism Policing said he is now in US custody over suspected national security and espionage allegations. At the time of his arrest, Russia said it had "nothing to do with it".British police previously said he was being held in London after he was arrested under section one and section three of the National Security Act 2023, which relate to obtaining or disclosing protected information, and assisting a foreign intelligence service.The day after Tyner's arrest on 10 November, Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said he was "unaware" of what it was connected to. "We have nothing to do with it, and it has nothing to do with us," he told reporters in Moscow.Image source, AFP via Getty ImagesImage caption, The US serviceman is understood to have been based at Imjin Barracks in GloucestershireOn Tuesday, Assistant Commissioner Laurence Taylor, head of Counter Terrorism Policing, said: "Subsequently, a decision was made to pass the investigation to them [their American partners] to progress.""These are extremely serious allegations, and our collective response should send a strong message that we will act swiftly and robustly where we suspect this kind of espionage activity taking place," he added.Tyner's arrest was the result of a long-running operation by MI5 - the UK's domestic intelligence and security agency - in collaboration with the FBI, the BBC understands.He had previously served in Afghanistan and Iraq, but at the time of his arrest was working with NATO's Allied Rapid Reaction Corps near Gloucester - where he was said to be entrusted with sensitive information which would have been extremely damaging if leaked to Russia.Detectives sent the Crown Prosecution Service a file on the senior US soldier's alleged spying for consideration - allegations described by the head of Counter Terrorism Policing as "extremely serious."But at that stage the Attorney General's Office in London got involved. As did the US authorities.And now the decision has been taken that Lieutenant Colonel Tyner should be taken into custody by the US Military.It means he will not stand trial in the UK, but under US Uniform Code of Military Justice.FBI director Kash Patel said an army officer was in custody "as the result of an espionage investigation and the close cooperation" between the bureau, US Army and various UK partners."Together we worked to identify a potential threat to national security and take swift action," he said. "This FBI has zero tolerance for anyone who betrays their oath to the United States or puts our national security at risk."US Brig Gen Sean Stinchon said the case should serve as a "stark warning to any service member suspected of violating the oath" they all take."Whenever we suspect somebody of betraying the trust of their fellow soldiers and jeopardising our collective defence, we will identify you, and we will ensure justice is served," he added.

schema.headline: American soldier arrested in UK taken into US military custody

title: Rubio says tech outages are not part of 'systemic attack' against US
description: US Secretary of State Marco Rubio has dismissed widespread concerns online that the series of recent tech outages in the past week are connected, tell
body: US Secretary of State Marco Rubio has dismissed widespread concerns online that the series of recent tech outages in the past week are connected, telling reporters there was "zero evidence" of any link.Rubio acknowledged that "people are fearful" the spate of outages, which included all flights being grounded in the US and widespread disruptions to banking, Apple and Microsoft services, could be linked or part of a plot."We are not under systemic attack," he said. "These events, one has nothing to do with the other, they are not inter-related."Cyber-security experts have agreed that there is no evidence linking the outages, and many of the issues appear due to updates to old infrastructure.In the past week, there has been a massive Microsoft outage, an apparent tech glitch which grounded all US flights for hours, and issues for the National Security Agency, outages affecting the biggest US banks and Apple. Every affected company or agency has said the issue was not cyber-related and not the work of an outside actor. Rubio's comments came hours after US Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton also addressed the issue, telling Fox News the outages were not the product of a cyber-attack. He explained "lots of institutions" are patching or upgrading systems, which has caused some disruption.Rubio was asked whether the Trump administration was concerned public fears could lead to stockpiling or a run on the banks.He said the best way to combat such fears was for the US government to share everything they know with the American people."Every indicator we have is that every single one of these events has an explanation or a cause that has nothing to do with a cyber-criminal, has nothing to do with a hostile actor or another country," he said.Cybersecurity experts say there is no evidence connecting the Microsoft, airline, and bank disruptions from the last five days.Kris Beevers, CEO and co-founder of the network and infrastructure management company NetBox Labs, acknowledged the circulating theories on social media linking the barrage of outages."There is no conspiracy here," he told the BBC."There is something more ordinary, and more important to understand: the infrastructure that runs the world is changing faster than ever, and change is risk. Much of it is 30 to 40 years old, with decades of technical debt, and it's now being asked to change very quickly."Beevers said AI is only part of the story."It's putting more strain on these legacy networks, and it's also creating real urgency around security," he said."Our customers are the amazing teams behind these networks at airlines, banking, energy, and retail who are essentially doing heart surgery on a global scale to get these networks back up and running quickly."Vice President of Threat Intelligence for Palo Alto Networks Unit 42, Sherrod DeGrippo, said: "What this week really underscores is how tightly coupled, and fragile, our core digital infrastructure is, where a single software bug or router failure can cascade nationwide."

schema.headline: Rubio says tech outages are not part of 'systemic attack' against US

title: Jeff Bezos was 'heavily involved' in Robert Pattinson's casting as Bond
description: Several other actors, including Josh O'Connor, Callum Turner and Jack Lowden, were reported to be in the frame for the role as screen tests took place
body: Several other actors, including Josh O'Connor, Callum Turner and Jack Lowden, were reported to be in the frame for the role as screen tests took place in recent weeks.But Amazon MGM ultimately went with a household name, choosing a more bankable movie star who is widely seen as a safe pair of hands."We ran a really tight process and made the final decision on Friday," Bezos said. There were five finalists who went through "real, old-fashioned screen tests", acting out three different scenes in full costume, with real sets and other actors, he said. "By the time we got to this list of five, they were all amazing. But there was something special about Rob and his performance," Bezos added. "It was immediately un-debated. Denis [Villeneuve], the director … we all gravitated toward Rob."The pick comes amid widespread Hollywood cuts and consolidation, with studios struggling to get people into cinemas. Hollywood insiders have said Pattinson was viewed as a safe pick to bring audiences in, rather than taking a risk on a new actor who could grow with the franchise. "Maybe he's boring. Maybe Hollywood would be passing up a chance to anoint a badly needed new star. But with so much at stake for everyone involved, that all makes him the obvious pick," Hollywood journalist Matthew Belloni, who predicted the pick, wrote in his newsletter. The BBC's Regan Morris contributed to this report.

schema.headline: Jeff Bezos was 'heavily involved' in Robert Pattinson's casting as Bond

title: Out of work and not in college: How quickly could Milburn's ideas help you?
description: Image source, Getty ImagesByHayley ClarkeEducation reporterAlan Milburn has said the country needs a "complete system reset" to bring down the number
body: Image source, Getty ImagesByHayley ClarkeEducation reporterAlan Milburn has said the country needs a "complete system reset" to bring down the number of young people not in work or education - known as "Neets".In a major review, published on Tuesday,, external he suggested a raft of proposals to address the problem, which mostly cover England but he says can be adapted in Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland too.Each of his recommendations will need to be accepted by the government and implemented and paid for before they become reality - and that could take some time. So how might today's proposals affect you if you are Neet?A new Youth Opportunity ServiceAt the heart of the recommendations, Milburn says, is a new Youth Opportunity Service. He wants this to be implemented locally, with each area drawing up a plan to help their own young people.It would bring together employment, careers, health and practical support, with each young person getting a named adviser and a personalised plan.Milburn wants areas to begin building their Youth Opportunity Service from 2027, with one in place everywhere by the end of 2029.Within 14 days of entering the service, a young person would then meet with a named adviser. Within four weeks, they would have their "personalised participation plan", setting out what both the support services and the young person involved would do, and when.Jobs wise, Milburn wants there to be initiatives like work placements of up to 12 weeks, structured volunteering opportunities, and help to create businesses.He also wants those who remain Neet - despite enagaging with support - to be provided with a paid six-month job, funded by the government.The government has already committed to a legal guarantee of job support in theory, but the exact workings still need to be worked out.More apprenticeships and college placesAlongside more work opportunities, Milburn wants a "major expansion" in further education for 18- to 24 year-olds, as well as more apprenticeship places.Over the next decade, he wants the number of young people completing an apprenticeship to double, and for apprenticeships to rival university as an option for school leavers.Colleges should also get new funding for participation and work-readiness, the review says, initially targeted at 16- and 17-year-olds who are Neet or at serious risk of becoming so.He also wants the government to develop new industry-led technical colleges and specialist campuses.If the reforms are enacted, Milburn says young people should have better access to high-quality further education and apprenticeships by 2028.Under the proposals, schools, colleges and universities would be judged by whether pupils make successful transitions into further learning and work, rather than just academic achievements.By 2036, he wants 35% of each year group to have started a high-quality apprenticeship by age 25.More mental health supportMilburn has said he wants a fundamental transformation of how mental health support for young people is delivered.Young people who are Neet should be guaranteed fast-track access to services within three months, according to his recommendations. This would include things like vocational rehabilitation, talking therapies and counselling as part of a young person's plan with their local Youth Opportunity Service - which would be rolled out between 2027 and 2029 under the plans.There has been a big rise in mental distress among children and young people in recent years, and Milburn's report comes at a time the NHS is facing huge pressures.Milburn wants mental health support to be available for all young people digitally, without needing a diagnosis.Some areas are already using these approaches, but scaling them up would be a major challenge and would take a long time to introduce across the board.Plus, Milburn wants "fitness to work" notes to be taken out of the hands of GPs and put into community work and health teams, and for them to be "a trigger for help - not simply a certificate of absence".Milburn wants these changes to begin in 2027 and would be linked to the Youth Opportunity Service rollout, which would be complete by 2029 under the plans.More incentives for employers to hire young peopleMilburn has said he wants companies to be incentivised to employ more young people, with the report highlighting a competitive jobs market and applicants who often fail to hear back from potential employers.The report includes three asks of employers: to create more genuine first jobs, more first-job apprenticeships and much wider access to meaningful work experience.Plus, Milburn wants large employers to find ways of responding to rejected job applicants.These changes should be felt by both employers and the young people looking for jobs by 2029, the report says.To achieve this, the report suggests a £3,000 payment for employers who take on someone who has been Neet for six months, with a further premium of £2,000 available if they are a small business.An extra payment of £2,000 would go to employers taking on somebody taking substantially greater barriers, such as care leavers or disabled young people.These payments are proposed to be part of changes to the Youth Jobs Grant - which already exists, external - but they would expand under Milburn's proposals from 2027.Get in touchShare your experiences and ask your questions.

schema.headline: Out of work and not in college: How quickly could Milburn's ideas help you?

title: Government backs welfare shake-up to prevent 'lost generation'
description: The government has backed plans by former minister Alan Milburn for sweeping reforms to prevent "losing a generation" of young people to a life on ben
body: The government has backed plans by former minister Alan Milburn for sweeping reforms to prevent "losing a generation" of young people to a life on benefits. Milburn proposes spending billions on tailored support for under 25s not in employment, education or training (Neets), to be part-funded by cuts to some benefits.He claims his plan, which also proposes tax breaks for firms and major education reforms, will get 440,000 young people into jobs by 2036. Prime Minister Andy Burnham said he endorsed the "principles" of the Milburn review and was confident he could persuade Labour MPs to back legislation to implement its measures.The PM told Sky News he would set out a full response to the review next month, after he had received a separate report into Personal Independence Payments (Pips) by Social Security Minister Sir Stephen Timms.But he added: "I have never in my years in politics seen a wholesale, whole government approach to supporting the next generation."That is what this represents, and I am absolutely confident that I can take this vision and get people behind it, indeed get the country behind it, because we will not place Britain in the position I want it to be in if we have a generation of young people growing up without hope for the future."The government has made Milburn the head of a new new youth opportunities unit to deliver on his recommendations.Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch said her party agreed with Milburn's "diagnosis" but claimed Labour had "made the problem much worse for young people" by increasing employers' National Insurance contributions and the youth minimum wage.There are few signs so far that Burnham will face a backlash from his own MPs of the scale that blocked his predecessor Sir Keir Starmer's planned £5bn welfare cuts last year.But some left-wing Labour MPs and the Unison trade union have warned proposals to cut health-related benefits will drive some young people into poverty.Work and Pensions Secretary Pat McFadden told MPs that "in future" the welfare state should be judged "not just by a snapshot of people's monthly incomes" but "but by the story of people's lives, and by their ability to achieve their full potential".McFadden, who was flanked by Burnham and Chancellor John Healey during his statement in the Commons, said the government rejected claims that young people were "snowflakes and shirkers".The million who were not in work or training had been robbed of the "prospect of a good future" and that was something that demanded "much more" than a conventional government response, he told MPs.He said the government would publish draft proposals on welfare reform early next year, with legislation to follow.In his wide-ranging 250 page report, external, Milburn proposes:An "entirely new benefits system" for under-25s, which would end the health-top up of Universal Credit and Personal Independence Payments (Pip), the main disability benefit in England and WalesInstead, a new "youth allowance" would be set at the basic rate of Universal Credit for under-25s, with a higher rate for those living independentlyA reduction in employers' National Insurance costs for 21- to 24-year-olds, starting in the retail and hospitality sectors, meaning employing those young people would be cheaperA huge expansion in post-18 college places and a legal right to work, education or trainingA new, locally-led Youth Opportunity Service in England to give young people one named advisor and a personalised participation planPrimary and secondary schools required to identify and support pupils at risk of becoming Neet, and schools obliged to offer work experienceThe report calls for the government to spend around £5.8bn in total by 2036-37 on extra mental health and employment support.And it urges ministers to "kickstart the reform programme" next year, with an initial £500m, from "repriotising" existing spending.Milburn has said his plans are not about saving money - and his report says the government will not see overall savings from reduced benefit bills and higher tax receipts until 2036/27, when it will claw back £200m.But by then, it assumes the share of 16–24-year-olds that are Neet will have gone down from 13% - one of the highest in Europe - to 5%, the lowest in the UK since records began.Launching his report earlier on Tuesday, Milburn said "half measures will not do" because "the scale of the problem is just too big for that".He added: "Britain is at risk of losing a generation of young people, not because they lack talent, not because they lack ambition, not because they do not want to work."This is not a crisis of aspiration; it is a crisis of opportunity."Milburn's report has no specific blueprint for Scotland, Wales or Northern Ireland, where education, skills, health and local government are devolved.He said the UK and devolved governments "should agree common definitions, a shared set of headline outcomes and a regular joint review of progress".Scotland's Education Secretary Màiri McAllan said: "Where there is opportunity to collaborate with the UK government and others for the benefit of young people in Scotland, we will take it."But she argued many of the reforms recommended for England, such as stronger vocational training, were already in place in Scotland. A spokesperson for the Welsh government said: "We stand ready to work with the UK government to ensure Wales benefits fully from any UK-wide measures that improve life chances through access to rewarding work."Reform UK leader Nigel Farage said he agreed "with the general drift of the Milburn report, but it's too little and too slow". "We have a fundamental problem in Britain," he added. "Too many people are being encouraged to go on benefits, and training and apprenticeship schemes that take far too long."Lib Dem treasury spokesperson Daisy Cooper said if the government wanted to get people into work, it should back high street firms "that give many their first job", scrap the "unfair jobs tax" and negotiate a new growth and defence partnership with the EU.Green Party leader Zack Polanski described Milburn's proposals as a "flimsy sticking plaster" that intend to "slash support for disabled young people while subsidising corporations to hire cheap labour".

schema.headline: Government backs welfare shake-up to prevent 'lost generation'

title: Nations League: Belief and bench help Northern Ireland to League A promotion
description: After going 500 minutes without conceding a goal, Northern Ireland could be forgiven for having to make adjustments to play from behind. Having travel
body: After going 500 minutes without conceding a goal, Northern Ireland could be forgiven for having to make adjustments to play from behind. Having travelled to Budapest knowing a point against Hungary would be enough to top Nations League B2, Barnabas Varga's strike after 35 minutes for the hosts at the Puskas Arena altered the picture and, for the first time in the campaign, left Michael O'Neill's side having to chase a game.Their response to the deficit - on the pitch, from the bench and high in the stands where their suspended manager was watching the game - displayed the best characteristics of a side who had not won at this level before this unbeaten campaign.While the point from a 1-1 draw in Budapest will be long remembered for Justin Devenny's brilliant equaliser and the scenes of celebration that greeted promotion to the competition's top tier for the first time, it was beyond the highlights and headlines that O'Neill saw the emerging qualities of his side."We went behind tonight and it was difficult, you know? Big stadium, big atmosphere, but we came out and played well in the second half and got what we needed from the game," said the manager."Those are things that I'm very pleased that are in this squad at such a young age. The technical side of the game we'll always look to improve on, but in terms of the physical, the tactical and the mental side of a game, we're very far ahead of where I thought we would be at this time."For all the plaudits earned by this team who conceded just one goal in six games while picking up 12 points, among the most impressive aspects of the campaign has been who they have had to do without.Talismanic Liverpool defender Conor Bradley has not played for this side in over 12 months through injury.Ali McCann is another who missed both 2026 Nations League windows, while influential defender Daniel Ballard featured only in the first game in Georgia before a hamstring injury.Arsenal's Ceadach O'Neill was forced to pull out of the November squad through injury at a time when he would perhaps have been the most natural replacement for Jamie Donley after the striker picked up a second booking against Ukraine last week and had to miss the finale through suspension.Having taken over an ageing squad four years ago, O'Neill has rebuilt his playing panel with a group that feels as if it is getting deeper with each international window."The encouraging thing is we have players on the outside - we've Bradley to come back in, Ballard to come back in, Ali McCann, young Ceadach, Eoin Toal," added the former Stoke City and Blackburn Rovers boss."We have good competition for places now. We're going to need that competition, and some players are going to miss out, but we are building depth to the squad that will help us going forward."Come the next Nations League, that will be all the way into the uncharted territory of the top tier.

schema.headline: Nations League: Belief and bench help Northern Ireland to League A promotion

title: Nvidia reports bumper results as firm says it's not reinstating Jensen Huang
description: Nvidia's quarterly sales doubled to top $100bn for the first time as the company insisted it has no plans to reinstate ousted co-founder Jensen Huang.
body: Nvidia's quarterly sales doubled to top $100bn for the first time as the company insisted it has no plans to reinstate ousted co-founder Jensen Huang.In the company's first results since Huang's dramatic exit, interim chief executive Colette Kress said it is "business as usual" and told investors: "We've got this." The company's quarterly sales doubled from a year earlier, reaching $115.8bn (£86.9bn), with shares in the company jumping by 4.8% in after-hours trading. Earlier on Tuesday, Huang said he would be "honoured" to return and lead Nvidia, having quit following alleged extramarital affairs, including one with a suspected spy for China."The board does not intend to reinstate him," Nvidia chair Harvey Jones said during a call on Tuesday with financial analysts. The company's profits also doubled from a year ago. For the quarter, which covered the three months to 25 October, profit hit $65bn. Its revenue from data centres, a significant part of Nvidia's business, also doubled to $107bn in the same period.Going forward, the company said its rapid growth is poised to continue, and revenue will rise by another 13% in the next quarter. Given the uncertainty surrounding the company after Huang's exit, financial analysts had been unsure that Nvidia would provide any forward-looking guidance. Daniela Hathorn, a senior analyst for trading platform Capital.com, said Nvidia's results "offer a strong answer to concerns that demand for AI infrastructure is cooling" and temper immediate worries that Huang was irreplaceable as a leader."The harder question is whether Nvidia can preserve the strategic advantage Huang helped build," Hathorn added. "His exit is unlikely to change orders already committed, but could matter more when Nvidia makes its next round of decisions on products, partnerships and investment."Kress seemed eager to stress that Nvidia can continue to not only succeed, but lead the ongoing AI buildout that is happening throughout the technology industry."It is business as usual," she said. "Our partners, our suppliers, all of them are 100% behind us."She added that Nvidia's leadership team has "stood up very strongly over the last week... working seamlessly in all of their departments and projects"."Our momentum is real. Our demand is accelerating. Our supply is growing. Our customers and our partners are with us, and employees are committed." Kress said before leaving the analyst call. "We've got this."The interim CEO also said Nvidia is no longer shipping Hopper data centre semiconductors to China.The Hopper technology is in Nvidia's advanced H200 processors, which the firm won approval to sell in China after Huang's repeated lobbying efforts in Washington.They had previously been restricted over concerns that selling them to China would give its industries and military an edge over the US.Kress did not elaborate on why the shipments had been stopped.

schema.headline: Nvidia reports bumper results as firm says it's not reinstating Jensen Huang

title: Cricket Australia sets up 'safe space' for players to share sandpapergate experiences
description: Cricket Australia has launched an independent "forum" for players and staff involved in the sandpapergate scandal to share their version of events.In
body: Cricket Australia has launched an independent "forum" for players and staff involved in the sandpapergate scandal to share their version of events.In a memoir released earlier this month, former player Usman Khawaja claimed the entire Australia team knew of the plot to tamper with the ball during a 2018 Test in South Africa, contradicting the investigation at the time.His comments have led to a bitter split among former and current players and have overshadowed the beginning of Australia's international cricket season.The forum was not a new investigation and there will be no new penalties, Cricket Australia said, adding that nobody would be forced to take part.However, chief executive Todd Greenberg said he hoped the discussions would allow the sport to "move on"."The game is genuinely hurting at the moment. It's not good for anyone," he said."We need to find a path through and we need some time to heal."The sandpapergate scandal is often described as one of Australian cricket's darkest days and was a source of national shame.An expedited investigation at the time found three players knew about the plan: captain Steve Smith, vice-captain David Warner and fellow batter Cameron Bancroft. They all faced lengthy bans.However Khawaja, Warner and another player on the tour, Chadd Sayers, have all now said they believe everyone knew.Current Australia captain Pat Cummins has rejected claims he knew sandpaper was being taken onto the field as "nonsense", and expressed hurt that Khawaja - his friend - had called his reputation into question.The release of Khawaja's book has also renewed scrutiny of Cricket Australia's initial investigation. A handful of players - including the batter - have said they were not interviewed for it, and Warner has accused the governing body of a "cover-up"."Over the past week we've had several different and conflicting accounts of what transpired in Cape Town in 2018 and it's been an incredibly difficult and uncomfortable time for the game and for everyone who was involved," Greenberg said on Wednesday."What's become clear is that some players were not heard at that time. That opportunity now exists in a place without judgement, without sanction."Terms of reference for the forum are being drafted, he said, and a former judge or "someone of that ilk" will be recruited to run it, confidentially and independently.No deadline has been set, but Greenberg said he hoped the discussions could be completed "quickly", at which time the Cricket Australia board would decide what information to make public."We will look to be as transparent as we possibly can, whilst at the same time protecting the confidentiality of the people who come forward."The incident had "a lot to do with the culture that existed back at the time", Greenberg said: a win-at-all-costs mentality which he admitted the governing body played a role in creating.He added that it is important the current Australian team be "afforded the space to perform at their best at what is a very important time and period for the game". Though players like Khawaja and Warner have retired from international cricket, Australia's bowling attack in the contentious third Test - Pat Cummins, Josh Hazlewood, Nathan Lyon and Mitchell Starc - remain fixtures in the national side. So too does Steve Smith, who returned to the team in 2019.Khawaja, who is commentating Australia's one-day international against England in Hobart on Wednesday alongside Warner, welcomed the announcement."I wish Cricket Australia would have done this a week-and-a-half ago, probably longer ago," Khawaja said on streamer Kayo Sports."My questions will always be 'what is the outcome from this?'"Warner said Australians deserved an "open public inquiry" instead."Because we have no idea about what's happened behind closed doors with CA [Cricket Australia]."Former player turned coach Jason Gillespie and Darren Lehmann - who coached Australia at the time of the scandal - both said the forum was a good idea."Let's not beat around the bush - they didn't have a choice. Cricket Australia had to do something, the drums were beating louder and louder," Gillespie told the broadcaster ABC."I haven't been great and the people close to me know that... The last couple of weeks have been tough, but they have been for everyone," Lehmann added.

schema.headline: Cricket Australia sets up 'safe space' for players to share sandpapergate experiences

title: Pakistani man sentenced to 27 years for Iran-backed plot to kill Trump
description: A Pakistani man with ties to Iran's government has been sentenced to 27 years in prison for his role in a plot to assassinate US President Donald Trum
body: A Pakistani man with ties to Iran's government has been sentenced to 27 years in prison for his role in a plot to assassinate US President Donald Trump and other officials.Asif Merchant was found guilty in March of attempting to commit an act of terrorism transcending national boundaries and murder for hire after trying to hire hitmen to kill Trump, former President Joe Biden, and former US ambassador to the United Nations Nikki Haley.The hitmen were instead undercover FBI agents.In court, he said he was acting under the direction of Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) to avenge the 2020 US assassination of Qasem Soleimani, Iran's topmost military commander.New York US federal judge Eric Ross Komitee sentenced Merchant on Tuesday to 330 months (27 years and six months) in prison, months after a jury handed its guilty verdict.Although other US officials were potential targets, the assassination plot was largely focused on Trump because he was president at the time Soleimani was killed. Trump has spoken publicly about ordering the US airstrike that killed the Iranian general while he was travelling in Iraq.In response to the killing, Iran's late Supreme Leader Ayatollah Ali Khamenei said "severe revenge awaits the criminals" behind the attack.Prosecutors said Merchant initially travelled to Iran for religious pilgrimages and he was then introduced to an IRGC handler. He travelled to Iran 15 times where he received training from Iranian intelligence officers, prosecutors said, before flying to the US in April 2024 to carry out the plot.Prosecutors said Merchant paid $5,000 to the undercover hitmen as part of an initial payment. He was arrested in July 2024 in Texas as he was about to leave the US.In court, Merchant argued that he "had no other option" than to go along with the plot because his handler indicated that he knew who Merchant's Iranian relatives were and where they lived.He said he had anticipated being arrested before anyone was killed and intended to cooperate with the US government, CBS, the BBC's US partner reported. He had hoped that would help him obtain a green card.The jury deliberated for less than two hours before returning its verdict, US media said."An Iranian agent who came to the United States to coordinate an assassination attempt against President Trump has been justly sentenced for his criminal conduct," Attorney General Todd Blanche said in a statement. "The Department of Justice will not tolerate foreign terrorist plots against our leaders and will not stop until those responsible are held accountable."Additional reporting by Nardine Saad.

schema.headline: Pakistani man sentenced to 27 years for Iran-backed plot to kill Trump

title: Hunger Games prequel splits opinion: 'Surreally awful' or 'surprisingly strong'
description: Image source, LionsgateImage caption, Joseph Zada plays Haymitch Abernathy at the age of 16ByIan YoungsCulture reporterReviews of the latest Hunger Ga
body: Image source, LionsgateImage caption, Joseph Zada plays Haymitch Abernathy at the age of 16ByIan YoungsCulture reporterReviews of the latest Hunger Games film have seen it dismissed as a "surreally awful prequel" and "a tortuous, costly mess" by some critics - but called "surprisingly strong" and "one of the best films in the series" by others.The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping is the sixth movie in the franchise, and tells the origin story of a teenage Haymitch Abernathy - who was played as an adult by Woody Harrelson.In a one-star review, the Guardian called the film, external "overwrought and boring", and said it "has no actual interest and no authentic reason to exist, other than to gouge an income stream out of its fanbase".But the Wrap praised its, external "memorable performances, intoxicating style and horrifying commentary", adding: "When the dust settles it may even be the Hunger Games that holds up best."Image source, Murray Close/LionsgateImage caption, Ralph Fiennes stars as President SnowSunrise on the Reaping is set 24 years before the first Hunger Games film, and 40 years after the previous prequel, 2023's The Ballad of Songbirds and Snakes."This prequel lands at some mid-point between Ballad and Hunger Games, which puts it on an immediately odd footing," Empire said in a three-star review, external."It can't escape the sense of feeling supplementary. It's an enjoyable-enough diversion, but essentially a footnote with aspirations."Screen Daily called it, external an "underwhelming prequel", which "suffers from a lack of compelling characters" and "feels oddly incidental - a drab afterthought rather than a crucial new chapter".Image source, Murray Close/LionsgateImage caption, Kieran Culkin plays Hunger Games host Caesar FlickermanThe film's all-star cast includes Ralph Fiennes, Jesse Plemons, Glenn Close, Kieran Culkin, Elle Fanning, Mckenna Grace and Maya Hawke alongside Joseph Zada as the 16-year-old Abernathy.IndieWire, external said Zada's performance is "charming enough", but "his character lacks the gravitational charisma or arc that, say, Jennifer Lawrence brought to the original films".The movie feels "a little bit like a cold cash grab rather than a necessary deepening of the series' lore" and is "a dreary slog", IndieWire's critic wrote.The New York Times, external also used the word "slog", adding: "One really misses the guiding presence of Jennifer Lawrence, who had the raw pathos to both ground and expand a world in a way many younger stars often can't."In Sunrise, we're instead left with fleeting moments in which Plemons or Ralph Fiennes (playing the evil President Snow) briefly elevate the film. They seem to be trapped in this dystopia too."Image source, Murray Close/LionsgateImage caption, The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping will be released this weekendHowever, the Hollywood Reporter, external was more enthusiastic about both the film and Zada's performance, calling it a "star-making turn".Its critic concluded: "Sunrise on the Reaping is a return, after the disappointing Songbirds and Snakes, to the spirit of the first movies."And Time Out's four-star review, external said the film is "as strong as any" of the other movies, and "certainly a major step up from 2023's drab prequel The Ballad of Songbirds and Snakes".

schema.headline: Hunger Games prequel splits opinion: 'Surreally awful' or 'surprisingly strong'

title: Philippines police ask prosecutors to charge Thomas Markle over child sex abuse material
description: Police in the Philippines have asked prosecutors to charge Thomas Markle Sr, the father of Meghan, Duchess of Sussex, with possession of and intent to
body: Police in the Philippines have asked prosecutors to charge Thomas Markle Sr, the father of Meghan, Duchess of Sussex, with possession of and intent to distribute child sexual abuse material.Cebu province prosecutor Graeme Elmido told the BBC that police had filed documents requesting that Markle be charged on Monday.Earlier this month, Markle, 82, was separately arrested and charged in the US with possession of child sexual abuse material. The FBI said agents seized about 78 items, including film negatives, slides and books that they allege contained child sex abuse material, from storage units Markle rented.Markle, who is in custody in the US, has previously denied the allegations. The BBC has contacted Markle's attorney for comment.Elmido told the BBC that Philippine National Police had asked prosecutors to charge Markle with "two counts of intent to distribute CSAEM [child sexual abuse and exploitation material], and one count of possession of CSAEM material".Last month, police in the Philippines obtained a warrant to examine devices allegedly removed from Markle's former home in the country.Four boxes of material, including computers, phones, hard drives and old video tapes, were handed to officers by Meghan's half brother Thomas Markle Jr.Earlier this month, Markle Sr was arrested and charged in the US. He had initially been placed under house detention at his assisted living facility in Florida, but was taken back into custody last week after prosecutors alleged he removed his ankle monitor. Meghan Markle has been estranged from her father since 2018. The BBC understands she broke contact with him last year, telling him she and the authorities knew he had abused young girls.In a previously shared statement after the allegations against her father emerged, Meghan wrote: "I am deeply distressed... my thoughts are with any children who may have been harmed."She said she hoped it could be understood why she had largely cut off contact from her father and did "not allow him to have contact with our children".

schema.headline: Philippines police ask prosecutors to charge Thomas Markle over child sex abuse material

title: Waymo temporarily pulls driverless taxis from all US freeways
description: Waymo has temporarily suspended its driverless vehicles from operating on all US freeways, the company has said.The decision comes after California ba
body: Waymo has temporarily suspended its driverless vehicles from operating on all US freeways, the company has said.The decision comes after California banned Waymo's driverless taxis from state freeways following a series of recent traffic incidents.California's Department of Motor Vehicles (DMV) cited an "imminent hazard to public safety" for the ban, noting an incident this month in which several driverless Waymo vehicles entered an active construction zone on US Route 101.Waymo said it was working with state officials "diligently and responsibly to resume freeway operations", adding that no injuries or collisions were reported following the incident on US Route 101 south of San Francisco.California's DMV said Waymo's driverless taxis presented a risk "due to recurring incursions by its vehicles into active construction zones where construction workers, vehicles and equipment are present".In another incident earlier this month, footage widely seen on social media appeared to show a Waymo car trying to overtake patrol vehicles that were deliberately slowing the pace of traffic on a San Francisco highway.The California ban, which came into effect on 11 November, would remain in place until Waymo "demonstrates to the department that it has taken effective corrective actions to address the deficiencies that precipitated the restrictions".A Waymo spokesperson said: "In alignment with our safety-first principles, we have also temporarily restricted freeway operations across our other operating markets to evaluate our performance."Data on Waymo's website suggests that its cars, compared to human drivers, are involved in 95% fewer crashes resulting in serious injury.Waymo currently operates driverless taxis in 15 US cities, but only offered freeway rides in a handful of those locations, including San Francisco, Los Angeles and Miami.The company's driverless taxis can continue to operate on regular city streets.In May, Waymo recalled thousands of its self-driving cars in the US over a software issue that could allow vehicles to drive into flooded roads.In the same month, multiple Waymo cars were spotted driving around a cul-de-sac in Atlanta, Georgia, in the early hours of the morning.

schema.headline: Waymo temporarily pulls driverless taxis from all US freeways

title: Cutting EV target risks UK missing climate targets, warns adviser
description: The UK is likely to miss legally binding climate targets if the government reduces electric vehicle (EV) targets, independent adviser the Climate Chan
body: The UK is likely to miss legally binding climate targets if the government reduces electric vehicle (EV) targets, independent adviser the Climate Change Committee (CCC) has warned.In a letter to Transport Secretary Heidi Alexander, the CCC argues that weakening the targets would result in "economic and energy security costs" and leave households "more exposed to volatile fossil fuel prices". The CCC says that switching to an electric vehicle can save a typical household around £800 a year, with fewer people benefiting if the targets were watered down.The warning comes after weeks of speculation that the government plans to announce changes to the EV targets. Government sources insist no decision has been made.Under the current rules, a "zero emission vehicle" (ZEV) mandate requires 80% of new cars sold in the UK to be zero emission by 2030 and all new cars to meet that standard by 2035. Companies that fail to meet their ZEV mandate face a potential fine of £12,000 per car, although there are exemptions. Industry groups have long complained the current rules impose too heavy a burden, calling instead for a "sustainable transition".Latest data from trade body the Society of Motor Manufacturing and Traders (SMMT) shows that EVs, as well as plug-in hybrids, are driving growth in new car sales. In the year so far, 26.6% of all new car registrations have been fully electric, the SMMT says, which is below the headline target of 33% for 2026.But the industry as a whole appears on course to comply with this year's mandate once flexibilities are accounted for, according to analysis by New AutoMotive, a transport research organisation which supports the transition to electric carsSMMT Chief Executive Mike Hawes accused the CCC of ignoring the costs of the targets it was defending. "The industry cannot subsidise the transition indefinitely, which is why it is unified in seeking change," he said.The CCC analysis also argued that weakening the targets would lead to a hole in the government's carbon savings that need to be made in order to meet its legally binding climate targets. The CCC said the ZEV mandate "underpins the largest share of emissions reduction to 2037" in the government's net-zero plan.  The climate targets set for 2033-2037 will be missed "without alternative action at the same scale", the CCC argued.CCC analysis shows surface transport - which includes cars, vans and trucks - remains the country's highest carbon-emitting sector and one of the slowest to decarbonise. Lord Deben, former CCC chairman, said going against CCC advice would "not be sensible" as it would "cost people money". He said climate targets were "not random targets" and "if you don't reach them then you put yourselves in really serious danger of having climate change, which we can't handle".A government spokesperson said: "We remain committed to the phase out of all new petrol and diesel cars by 2030 and to all new car and van sales being zero emission by 2035, as well as to our legally binding net zero targets. Our consultation on the Mandate will not change this and will ensure we are taking a pragmatic and balanced approach to the ZEV transition."

schema.headline: Cutting EV target risks UK missing climate targets, warns adviser
